lines.text: Investigators, journalists, lawyers and researchers share one problem.
Too much evidence to read, and a result nobody can later prove was not changed.
Sealbook is an app for exactly that. It works in three steps.
You bring the material in. The app reads all of it and proposes connections, each shown with the exact place it came from.
A person approves or declines each one with a signature, and the record is sealed, so anyone can check it later.
Four invented cases show how that helps.
One: a person under several names. Four desks at a freight company each keep a clean file: 14 sources and 1,445 sheet rows.
Kassar. Qassar. Khassar. Kasar. And on one licence, the name in Arabic.
Four spellings, two alphabets, one man. And one who is not him: a surveyor with the same name, born elsewhere.
The app proposed these links. Here, fixed rules with no AI model found 4 of the 6 true links, enough to join all his records.
A person declines the surveyor, and signs each decision with a passkey, a key on their own device.
The case closes on a signed conclusion, checked by a colleague, saying how sure it is and what is not established.
Two: a statement that does not fit. A bookkeeper says she was 34 kilometres from a fire. Exhibit sheets from her phone put her at the yard.
The app flags two places on one day. A person reads the times, and concludes she was there.
Three: an old clip shared as new. The app ties 8 of 9 reposts to a flood video from two years earlier, mostly by sound. One cropped, mirrored, muted copy is missed.
Four: a person who drops out of the record. A statement says when a bus driver was last seen. The app finds 73 days with no log naming him. A lead, not a finding.
Every decision is signed by a person. A court can check the sealed package offline; here, on a test package.
The machine reads more than a person can, and finds the links. A person approves every one.
